name: Carlos Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain stage-lighting cue software at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI every day to draft tests, but check cues against rehearsal recordings. Mina makes ceramics for shops, our children are grown, and typical developer pay has helped us rent with four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the lighting team that a little AI help with cue lists is convenient, but a lamp still has to come on when a performer reaches the mark. I use AI every day to draft code tests and check them against the rehearsal recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain stage-lighting cue software as an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company. Mina makes ceramics for local shops, our children are grown, and our typical pay has helped us rent with four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing one show cue against a rehearsal each week and log any delayed lamp. We would save 115 monthly while both wages arrive and repair the old bicycle rather than buy a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our jobs and bills here. A perfect cue list on a screen can still leave an actor in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cue failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stage lamp came up after the actor had already crossed the doorway. I found a time offset in the cue file and checked it at the next rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was your work before software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ran a small venue’s sound desk before moving into code. I know the timing of a show, though the lighting electricians know the wiring better than I do.

I use **AI daily** for draft tests, then verify the show.
think: I have **four months saved** from typical developer pay and Mina’s ceramics orders.
I see **rent covered** even when the shop buys fewer ceramics pieces.
do: **Keep testing show cues** weekly against rehearsal recordings.
**Save 115 monthly** while both wages arrive; repair old bicycle rather than replace it.

fieldNote: His **sound-desk past** supports timing knowledge without making him a lighting electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, planning, checking and coding could build many cue lists and tests. A technician still needs to approve a live lighting change around people on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid developer hours could shrink if the software writes its own cue checks. Four months saved and some local tech jobs give me time to react, but Mina’s ceramics income alone cannot carry our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for approved paid time to pilot a new AI cue-conflict checker on old rehearsal files, with the lighting technician reviewing the result. If approved, I’d test one conflicting cue each week; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local show-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours, but the tool is worth testing on a recording. An audience should not be the first test of a lighting change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What conflict would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a blackout and a spotlight cue at the same second. The technician would check which one is safe before any live show used the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run it during a performance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the trial on archived recordings until my lead and the technician approve it for use.

say: I want **technician sign-off** before AI changes a live theatre lighting cue.
I want **old rehearsals** used for testing before any audience sees the lighting tool.
think: I could lose **paid cue-testing hours** to automation.
I cannot rely on **Mina’s ceramics income** alone for rent.
do: **Pilot AI cue checker** weekly only with approved paid time, archived recordings and technician review.
**Search paid show-software vacancies** if hours fall and local wages cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but curious** about own paid hours.
S1.quote: An audience should not be the first test of a lighting change.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** goes beyond existing daily draft tests and requires paid approval.
A **local job search** starts only after reduced hours and a bill-covering paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write cue code and plan a show’s lighting cheaper than our team. Robots climbing rigs and moving scenery may arrive around 2031, after software work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my mid-level developer job could end despite knowing the show, and four months saved would not last through a long search. Mina’s ceramics orders can be uneven, so we cannot use them as a replacement salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone replacing the living-room floor and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local sound-desk vacancies only if my safety qualification is current, openings exist and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office what support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing a steady wage. A rehearsal can be repeated; a missed rent payment cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your sound-desk qualification current?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to check with venues before applying. I would not assume an old badge lets me run equipment today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a venue job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local theatres and tech firms first. Mina’s shop customers and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach cue code first.
I expect **rigging robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end quickly.
I know **four months saved** cannot cover a long search.
do: **Postpone floor replacement** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for sound-desk work** after 2028 loss only if cleared local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A rehearsal can be repeated; a missed rent payment cannot.
fieldNote: He checks **current venue qualifications** before treating old sound-desk work as a fallback.
Four months saved provides **limited search time** while physical rigging robots come later.

steps.text: Postpone living-room floor replacement when developer cuts threaten
Apply for qualified paid local sound-desk vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to check who will run physical shows while code changes. Robots climbing rigs and moving scenery may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could renew my venue safety badge while the developer wage lasts, though a badge does not create a show. I would not spend our four-month reserve without a paid shift lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a theatre for a paid sound-desk shift and ask my software employer to approve outside work. If a vacancy exists, the venue funds safety renewal and the shift pays enough for travel, I’d take one a month with the head technician checking my setup; we would save 100 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d apply for paid local sound work only if qualified openings cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about code work, but a paid show would tell me whether my hands still know the desk. A badge cannot turn up the sound by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the head technician check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician would check my cable paths, sound level and emergency mute before doors open. I would not sign off a live show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venue cannot fund renewal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer wage and wait for a paid opening that funds the requirement. I would not use rent savings for a speculative badge.

I expect **rigging robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could refresh **sound-desk work** on a paid shift.
I need **funded safety renewal** before treating it as income.
do: **Take paid sound shift** only with vacancy, funded safety renewal, travel pay, outside-work approval and head-technician review.
**Apply for sound work** after 2031 loss only if qualified local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but testing** a real paid shift.
S3.quote: A badge cannot turn up the sound by itself.
fieldNote: The **paid trial** requires a real shift, funded renewal, travel coverage and outside-work approval.
A later **sound job** remains conditional on qualification, local vacancies and bill-covering pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives venues time to train people for live equipment and families time to save. Robots on physical rigs may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not checked a retirement amount and do not know when I can stop paid work. Four months saved makes our bills safe now, but a lost software wage later would still need a real replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing lighting cues and save 120 monthly while both wages hold. I’d take a paid supervised sound shift quarterly only if a venue offers one, funds current safety requirements, covers travel and my software employer approves outside work; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local sound vacancies only if qualified wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about a later job change but secure in the next few years. A live show tells me whether the trade still fits; a career chart cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no venue has a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the software job and savings. I would not count a future show as income before a venue books and pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and Mina and I will fund our plans from work we actually have.

say: I want **paid live-show practice** before AGI reaches cue code in 2036.
I expect **rigging robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a verified figure.
I see **four months saved** as current security, not future wages.
do: **Keep testing cue software** while developer role pays.
**Save 120 monthly** while both wages hold; take paid supervised sound shifts only with vacancy, funded safety, travel pay, employer approval.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my developer wage could end before a qualified paid sound-desk opening appears. Written notice, a real local vacancy covering rent and verified temporary help would let us use our savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether an old sound-desk badge makes me ready for a live show. I would want a head technician to check my setup before the doors open.

headlineQuote: I would want a head technician to check my setup before the doors open.
portrait: Carlos is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and four months saved.
He and Mina **rent** while ceramics orders vary and grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but verifies cue tests against rehearsal recordings.
He tries **paid sound shifts** only with funded safety renewal, travel coverage, approval and supervision.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer wage before a qualified paid sound opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a local rent-covering vacancy and verified temporary public help would matter.
